suggestions.whyItIsHappening: {childName} is probably overstimulated or overtired. His nervous system is very sensitive right now and too much input can quickly become overwhelming.

steps.title: Move to a quieter, dimmer place
steps.instruction: Find the calmest room in the house. Dim the lights if you can. Remove any background noise — turn off the TV, step away from the kitchen.
steps.tip: Move slowly and speak quietly. Your calm body language directly affects his nervous system.

steps.title: Hold him against your chest
steps.instruction: Hold {childName} upright against your chest, his ear over your heart. Use a slow, rhythmic pat on his back.
steps.tip: Your heartbeat is the sound he heard for 9 months. It is the most calming thing in his world.

suggestions.fallback: Try offering a feed. Even if he fed recently, comfort sucking can help settle an overstimulated baby.

steps.title: Try the 5 S's — Swaddle
steps.instruction: Wrap {childName} snugly in a thin muslin — arms tucked in, not too tight.
steps.tip: Make sure his hips can still move freely inside the swaddle.

steps.title: Add gentle motion and shushing
steps.instruction: Hold the swaddled {childName} and gently rock or sway while making a continuous shushing sound — louder than you think you need to.
steps.tip: The shushing sound mimics the whooshing blood flow he heard in the womb.

steps.title: Try skin-to-skin contact
steps.instruction: Undress {childName} down to his nappy. Hold him against your bare chest and cover both of you with a light blanket.
steps.tip: Skin-to-skin regulates his temperature, heart rate, and stress hormones.

steps.title: Go outside briefly
steps.instruction: Fresh air and a change of environment can break the crying cycle.
steps.tip: The change in air temperature on his face is a gentle sensory reset.

suggestions.whyItIsHappening: {childName} may be overtired, hungry, or overwhelmed by a new skill or environment. Crying at this age is still his primary way to ask for help.

steps.title: Check the basics first
steps.instruction: Run through hunger, wet nappy, too hot or cold, and tiredness. Address the most likely need before trying anything else.
steps.tip: A quick HALT-style check saves time when you are stressed.

steps.title: Reduce stimulation
steps.instruction: Move to a quieter space. Put down your phone. Lower your voice and slow your movements around {childName}.
steps.tip: Your calm is contagious — rushing often prolongs the cry.

suggestions.fallback: If crying continues after basic needs are met, try a change of scenery — a walk outside or a different room.

steps.title: Offer comfort object or rhythm
steps.instruction: Try a familiar blanket, gentle rocking, or a short song you use at bedtime.
steps.tip: Predictable sensory input helps his nervous system settle.

steps.title: Stay close without fixing
steps.instruction: Sit nearby and let {childName} know you are there. You do not need to stop every sound immediately.
steps.tip: Sometimes babies need to discharge tension before they can reset.

steps.title: Try a movement reset
steps.instruction: Gentle bouncing on your knee, a slow walk, or a ride in the pram can shift his state.
steps.tip: Rhythmic movement mimics the womb and can break a crying loop.

steps.title: Pause and breathe together
steps.instruction: Hold {childName} and take three slow breaths yourself before the next attempt.
steps.tip: Regulating your body helps regulate his.

suggestions.whyItIsHappening: {childName} is feeling something he cannot express in words yet. Toddler crying is almost always communication, not manipulation.

steps.title: Get down to his level
steps.instruction: Kneel or sit so you are at his eye level. Just be present and calm.
steps.tip: Your physical presence and calm body is the regulation — not your words.

steps.title: Name the feeling out loud
steps.instruction: Say quietly: 'You are really upset right now. That is okay. I am right here.'
steps.tip: Naming an emotion activates the thinking part of his brain and reduces the intensity.

suggestions.fallback: If he is still inconsolable after 10 minutes, offer physical comfort — a hug, a familiar object, or a change of location.

steps.title: Offer a simple choice
steps.instruction: When he pauses, offer one small choice: this cup or that cup, this corner or the sofa.
steps.tip: Tiny control can reduce the intensity once he feels heard.

steps.title: Use a calm-down corner
steps.instruction: Guide him to a soft spot with a favourite toy. Stay nearby without demanding he stop crying.
steps.tip: A safe space teaches regulation over time — not in one moment.

steps.title: Change the scene
steps.instruction: Move to another room, step outside, or switch to water play at the sink.
steps.tip: A sensory shift can interrupt an emotional spiral.

steps.title: Reconnect after the storm
steps.instruction: When crying eases, offer a hug and one warm sentence: 'We got through that together.'
steps.tip: Repair builds trust — you do not need to lecture in the moment.

suggestions.whyItIsHappening: {childName} is probably overtired. Overtired babies find it harder to fall asleep because their stress hormones have kicked in.

steps.title: Create the right environment
steps.instruction: Dark room, white noise, cool temperature. These three things together signal sleep to his brain.
steps.tip: Darkness is the most important of the three.

steps.title: Start the wind-down before he needs it
steps.instruction: Start 10 to 15 minutes before you think he needs to sleep — a feed, a quiet hold, soft singing.
steps.tip: The Energy Bridge is designed to give you this 15-minute warning. Use that time.

suggestions.fallback: If he is fighting sleep, try a 5-minute reset — dim lights and hold him quietly before trying again.

steps.title: Use a consistent mini-routine
steps.instruction: Same order every time: nappy, feed, burp, swaddle, bed. Keep it short and predictable.
steps.tip: Babies learn sleep cues from repetition, not length.

steps.title: Place him down drowsy but awake
steps.instruction: When {childName} is heavy-eyed but not fully asleep, place him in the cot and pat rhythmically.
steps.tip: This builds the skill of falling asleep in the sleep space.

steps.title: Check for discomfort
steps.instruction: Gas, reflux, or being too hot can block sleep. Try upright hold for 10 minutes after a feed.
steps.tip: Sometimes sleep resistance is physical, not behavioural.

steps.title: Try motion then stillness
steps.instruction: A short walk or rock until calm, then transfer to cot with hand on chest for one minute.
steps.tip: Motion calms; stillness lets sleep arrive.

suggestions.whyItIsHappening: {childName} may be undertired, overtired, or excited by new milestones. Sleep resistance is common when the world feels too interesting.

steps.title: Watch wake windows
steps.instruction: Note how long he has been awake. Adjust bedtime earlier if he is rubbing eyes or fussy.
steps.tip: Catching the sleep window beats fighting past it.

steps.title: Keep the last 20 minutes boring
steps.instruction: No screens, no rough play, no new toys. Same low-key sequence every night.
steps.tip: Boring is good before bed.

suggestions.fallback: If he wakes frequently, check room temperature and whether he is going down overtired.

steps.title: Use a sleep cue object
steps.instruction: Introduce one soft item only for sleep — same blanket or toy in the cot each time.
steps.tip: Consistency helps his brain associate the object with sleep.

steps.title: Pat and pause
steps.instruction: Pat his back for 30 seconds, pause 10 seconds, repeat. Gradually reduce contact as he settles.
steps.tip: Small steps teach self-settling without leaving him alone abruptly.

steps.title: Address separation gently
steps.instruction: Stay in the room with a calm presence. Hum the same song each night.
steps.tip: Predictable presence reduces bedtime anxiety.

steps.title: Keep night feeds boring
steps.instruction: If he wakes to feed, keep lights low and interaction minimal.
steps.tip: Night is for sleep cues, not play.

suggestions.whyItIsHappening: Toddlers resist sleep because sleep means separation from you and the end of the exciting day.

steps.title: Start the routine earlier than you think
steps.instruction: Start the wind-down 30 minutes before you want him asleep. Bath, dim lights, quiet play, then the same bedtime sequence every night.
steps.tip: Predictability is everything.

steps.title: Give him one choice to feel in control
steps.instruction: Which pyjamas. Which book. Which side of the bed. One real choice is enough.
steps.tip: Give him tiny amounts of control and the big battles reduce.

suggestions.fallback: If bedtime stalls, shorten the routine but keep the order identical.

steps.title: Use a visual bedtime chart
steps.instruction: Three pictures: bath, book, bed. Point to each step as you do it.
steps.tip: Visual routines reduce negotiation.

steps.title: Set a clear last book rule
steps.instruction: Say: 'This is our last book, then sleep time.' Stick to it calmly.
steps.tip: Boundaries with warmth work better than endless extensions.

steps.title: Offer a comfort ritual
steps.instruction: Same goodnight phrase, same night-light, same stuffed friend every night.
steps.tip: Rituals signal safety when the day ends.

steps.title: Stay boring at the door
steps.instruction: If he calls out, return once with a brief reassurance, then less each night.
steps.tip: Consistency teaches that sleep is the expectation.

suggestions.whyItIsHappening: {childName} may be distracted, uncomfortable, or not hungry right now. Feeding patterns vary day to day in early months.

steps.title: Check comfort before feeding
steps.instruction: Burp, change nappy if needed, and make sure he is not overtired before offering a feed.
steps.tip: A comfortable baby feeds more easily.

steps.title: Reduce distractions
steps.instruction: Feed in a quiet, dim space. Put phones away and keep voices low.
steps.tip: Calm environment supports feeding reflexes.

suggestions.fallback: If refusal persists across multiple feeds, note timing and discuss with your health visitor.

steps.title: Try a different position
steps.instruction: Switch cradle hold, rugby hold, or slightly more upright if reflux is suspected.
steps.tip: Position can change comfort dramatically.

steps.title: Offer when sleepy-not-sleeping
steps.instruction: Catch the drowsy window after a nap when he may take a fuller feed.
steps.tip: Timing often matters more than technique.

steps.title: Skin-to-skin before feed
steps.instruction: Five minutes of skin contact can trigger feeding interest.
steps.tip: Closeness primes appetite in young babies.

steps.title: Stop and retry in 20 minutes
steps.instruction: If he turns away, pause and offer again shortly without pressure.
steps.tip: Forced feeds increase resistance.

suggestions.whyItIsHappening: Food refusal at this age is almost always developmental. {childName} is asserting independence through eating.

steps.title: Remove all pressure from mealtimes
steps.instruction: Put food on the tray and step back. No encouragement, no aeroplanes, no 'just one more bite'.
steps.tip: It can take 15 to 20 exposures to a new food before a toddler accepts it.

steps.title: Eat the same food yourself visibly
steps.instruction: If {childName} sees you eating something and genuinely enjoying it he is far more likely to try it.
steps.tip: Children this age learn almost entirely through imitation.

suggestions.fallback: Offer the same food again another day — novelty pressure backfires.

steps.title: Serve small portions
steps.instruction: Two or three pieces on the tray beats a full plate. Refill if he asks.
steps.tip: Small portions feel less overwhelming.

steps.title: Let him explore texture
steps.instruction: Allow touching, squishing, and smelling food without commenting.
steps.tip: Exploration is part of learning to eat.

steps.title: Keep milk on schedule
steps.instruction: Too much milk between meals can reduce appetite. Space feeds and solids thoughtfully.
steps.tip: Hunger is the best motivator for trying solids.

steps.title: End the meal calmly
steps.instruction: When he turns away, say 'All done' and clear the tray without drama.
steps.tip: Neutral endings prevent power struggles.

suggestions.whyItIsHappening: {childName} may be testing boundaries or filling up on snacks. Toddler appetite naturally varies week to week.

steps.title: Sit together at the table
steps.instruction: Family-style sitting — even for 10 minutes — improves willingness to try.
steps.tip: Meals are social before they are nutritional.

steps.title: Offer one safe food plus one new food
steps.instruction: Always include something he usually accepts alongside something new.
steps.tip: Safety plus novelty reduces refusal.

suggestions.fallback: Track patterns for a week before worrying — one picky day is normal.

steps.title: Limit grazing
steps.instruction: Structured snack times instead of constant crackers and fruit between meals.
steps.tip: Appetite needs space to build.

steps.title: Involve him in prep
steps.instruction: Stir, pour, or place food on plates — tiny jobs increase interest.
steps.tip: Participation creates ownership.

steps.title: Stay neutral about intake
steps.instruction: Do not praise eating or scold refusal. Describe what you see: 'You tried the carrot.'
steps.tip: Neutral feedback keeps food from becoming emotional currency.

steps.title: Close the kitchen after meals
steps.instruction: When mealtime ends, food is done until the next scheduled snack.
steps.tip: Clear boundaries reduce endless negotiation.
